newsitem.title: BURMA: Divisions run deep as Burma marks Union Day.
newsitem.headline: Divisions run deep as Burma marks Union Day.

text.p: Burma's military rulers and the opposition led by Aung San Suu Kyi held separate events to mark the golden jubilee of Union Day on Wednesday, signalling that political divisions still run deep in the multi-ethnic nation.

Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) party called for tripartite talks between the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), various ethnic groups and pro-democracy forces to build national reconciliation.

Prime Minister General Than Shwe, in an apparent reference to the Suu Kyi-led opposition and its western democracy supporters, urged ethnic groups to rise up and crush internal and external elements out to disturb Burma's progress.

Union Day marks the February 12, 1947, agreement signed by the various national races to form the Union of Burma and fulfill a condition set by the British colonial government to grant the country independence the following year.
But shortly after independence, several ethnic groups formed rebel factions and fought the Rangoon central goverment.

Amnesty International in a report released on Union Day said political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year reached their highest levels since the violent state suppression of a popular uprising at the end of the 1980s.
The human rights body said more than 2,000 people were arrested in 1996 for urging human rights reform, while it said opposition party members were also attacked by organised mobs.
Amnesty accused SLORC of "an almost complete intolerance of any peaceful political activity whatsoever".

About 10,000 people joined SLORC leaders at a government celebration in the People's Square in central Rangoon, while about 1,000 NLD supporters and some diplomats crowded into the grounds of Suu Kyi's lakeside residence to mark the day.

Also present at Suu Kyi's home were representatives of the Shan NLD and the Mon National Democratic Front. Burma is home to various national races including the Kachin, Kayah, Karen, Chin, Barma, Mon, Rakhine and Shan.

Than Shwe, in a message published in official media, said: "All the national brethren are urged to protect the stability and progess of the nation...to oppose and crush the internal and external elements who are disturbing and disrupting the progess of state."

He said 15 armed rebel groups had returned to the legal fold but made no mention of the Karen National Union (KNU) guerrilla group, which was formed in 1948 to seek more autonomy for the Karen state. It has refused to lay down arms.

Nobel peace laureate Suu Kyi invited various ethnic groups to meet the NLD and again labelled a government-organised National Convention of ethnic groups and military representatives to draft a new Burmese constitution a sham.
"We invite the nationality groups to come and have a meeting with the NLD because we, of course, represent the people of Burma. We received the mandate in the 1990 general election," she added.
The NLD swept to victory in the election but its victory was not recognised by the SLORC.
The SLORC gave permission for the ceremony at Suu Kyi's residence and allowed access to her home, to which roads have been blocked since December when student unrest broke out.
In Bangkok, about 20 exiled Burmese students staged a brief protest in front of the Burmese embassy and demanded that the SLORC relinquish power.
